solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A day before stag night, finally finds accommodation

indicators.note: before places the stag piece ahead of the closing letter, keeping answer order

parts.note: a stag night or stag party is for just men, so stag can mean exactly that

indicators.note: finally asks for the closing letter of the word night

explanation.surface: Someone finds a place to stay the day before a stag night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stag' reads as a noun in 'stag night', but here it stands alone as the adjective meaning men-only: JUST MEN.
explanation.definitionFit: An accommodation is an adjustment or compromise made to suit someone, as in reaching an accommodation.

clue.text: Excellent performance on Love Actually

indicators.note: in a down clue, on puts one piece above the next, so the performance sits on top of love

parts.note: def is slang for excellent or cool
an act is a performance on stage
love is zero in tennis, so the letter O

explanation.surface: A rave review for an excellent turn in the film Love Actually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love Actually' looks like the film title, but the two words split: Love gives O and Actually is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means 'in fact', describing what really exists rather than what is official.

clue.text: Generation following American custom

indicators.note: following places the generation piece after the American one

parts.note: US is short for American, as in US forces
a generation is an age or era

explanation.surface: A habit picked up by the generation that came after an American trend.
explanation.definitionFit: Usage is established practice or habit, the way things are customarily done.

clue.text: Oddly, they spilt the beans about hospital fund-raiser

indicators.note: Oddly asks for the first, third and further odd-placed letters of the word they
about means the confession phrase goes round the hospital letter

parts.note: to spill the beans is to let on, revealing a secret
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs

explanation.surface: Some people leaked secrets about a hospital charity appeal.
explanation.walkthrough: Oddly takes TE from 'they'; LET ON goes 'about' H to make LETHON.
explanation.definitionFit: A telethon is a long television broadcast that raises money for charity through viewers' pledges.

clue.text: Of great consequence, this could get at her?

parts.note: read the answer as an instruction: break up the word EARTH and its letters can give the two words at her

explanation.surface: Something momentous, perhaps aimed at a particular woman.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the answer, split as a word plus an anagram signal, is itself wordplay whose result is the clue's 'at her'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something world-changing in its impact is momentous, of huge significance.

clue.text: Drinks to nurse achieving success, for starters?

definitions.text: Drinks to nurse achieving success, for starters?

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold close, so the drinks hold the next letters inside

parts.note: tots are small measures of spirits

indicators.note: for starters asks for the opening letters of achieving and success

explanation.surface: Raising glasses to a nurse who has done well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to nurse' means hold inside, and 'for starters' takes opening letters. The whole clue also describes the occasion itself, which makes it an &lit.
explanation.definitionFit: To toast someone is to drink in their honour, often to celebrate an achievement.

clue.text: Opening wine, left harbour

definitions.meaning: an aperture, such as a porthole or a socket on a computer
the left-hand side of a ship, looking forward
a town or haven where ships dock

explanation.surface: Someone opened a bottle of wine as the ship left harbour.
explanation.definitionFit: One short word covers all four senses: an aperture, a fortified wine, a ship's left side and a harbour.

clue.text: Skin complaint, sir, is treated with soap

indicators.note: treated means the letters are processed or worked over into a new order

explanation.surface: A doctor tells a patient their skin problem is being dealt with using soap.
explanation.definitionFit: Psoriasis is a chronic skin disease causing red, scaly patches.

clue.text: Irritated, was first to go after row

indicators.note: to go after places the was-first piece behind the row piece

parts.note: a rank is a row, as in a taxi rank or ranks of soldiers
led means was in front, came first

explanation.surface: Someone was annoyed at having to go first after an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' looks like a quarrel, but it is a line: RANK.
explanation.definitionFit: Rankled is a verb meaning caused lasting resentment or annoyance.

clue.text: Refuse to part with pound for old ruler

indicators.note: to part with means giving up the pound letter

parts.note: offal is waste or refuse, especially from butchered animals
L is the pound sign, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Someone will not hand over a single pound to an ancient king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like a verb, but it is the noun meaning rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Offa was an eighth-century king of Mercia, famous for the earthwork Offa's Dyke.

clue.text: Look, almost no-one read novel — this one?

parts.note: lo is an old word for look, as in lo and behold

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are made into something new
almost means the last letter of no-one is dropped

parts.note: the letters of no-one as written

explanation.surface: Hardly anyone has read this novel, the clue laments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' signals an anagram of NOON (from 'almost no-one') plus READ, while 'this one?' points back to novel to define a famous book.
explanation.definitionFit: R. D. Blackmore's 1869 romance set on Exmoor is a classic English book, so it is one novel.

clue.text: Could be grave misfortune I had avoided

indicators.note: avoided means the I-had letters are kept out of the word

parts.note: an accident is a mishap or misfortune
I'd is the contraction of I had

explanation.surface: A serious calamity was narrowly dodged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grave' looks like serious; it is the grave mark over a letter, as in à.
explanation.definitionFit: A grave is one type of diacritic mark, alongside acute and circumflex.

clue.text: Town in Herts or maybe Balmoral area

parts.note: a Balmoral is a Scottish brimless cap, an example of headgear
a field is an area, as in a field of study

explanation.surface: A query about a town in Hertfordshire or the Royal estate at Balmoral.
explanation.walkthrough: Balmoral looks like the royal castle in Scotland, but it is also a Scottish cap. Herts is short for Hertfordshire, the county just north of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Hatfield is a town in Hertfordshire, home of Hatfield House.

clue.text: Small ducks found in river? Indeed

indicators.note: found in means the small ducks are placed inside the river

parts.note: the Forth is a Scottish river flowing into the Firth of Forth
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothes labels
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so a zero, the letter O; two of them

explanation.surface: Little ducks spotted on a river; how charming indeed.
explanation.definitionFit: Forsooth is an archaic word meaning truly or in truth, used for emphasis.

clue.text: One splits high cost with friend without complaining

indicators.note: splits means the one goes into the middle of the jumbled cost
high means intoxicated, so the letters of cost are in a mixed-up state

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
an ally is a friend or supporter

explanation.surface: Someone shares an expensive bill with a friend and does not grumble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'high' scrambles COST to STOC, which I 'splits' to give STOIC.
explanation.definitionFit: To act stoically is to endure hardship patiently, showing no sign of grumbling.

clue.text: Turf accountant's first to get drink

parts.note: a sod is a piece of turf

indicators.note: first asks for the opening letter of accountant's

explanation.surface: A bookmaker gets the first drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turf accountant' is old British slang for a bookmaker, but the two words split here.
explanation.definitionFit: Soda is fizzy water, a mixer or soft drink.

clue.text: Was upset by jokes about British surgeon

indicators.note: upset in a down clue turns the word over, reading it from the bottom up

parts.note: the word was as written
a one is a joke, as in 'have you heard the one about...', so jokes about are ones

explanation.surface: Someone was offended by jokes made about a British surgeon.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down light 'upset' means turned upside down, so it reads the first word from the bottom. 'jokes about' echoes the 'one about...' joke formula.
explanation.definitionFit: Sawbones is an old slang nickname for a surgeon or doctor, from amputations with a saw.

clue.text: Old ship's gone around river

indicators.note: around means the past word wraps round the river letter

parts.note: ago means gone by, in the past
R is the abbreviation for river on maps

explanation.surface: An old ship has gone round a river bend.
explanation.definitionFit: The Argo was the legendary vessel of Jason and the Argonauts.

clue.text: Not bothered by boring leader rambling

indicators.note: boring means drilling into, so the by letter goes inside
rambling means wandering, so the letters of leader wander out of order

parts.note: X means by, as in a room six by eight, 6x8

explanation.surface: Someone is unfazed by a dull, waffling boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boring' looks like dull; it means drilling into, putting X inside a jumble of LEADER.
explanation.definitionFit: Being relaxed means being calm and unconcerned, not worried.

clue.text: Rock star can't perform

indicators.note: to rock is to shake, so the letters are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: A rock star finds they are unable to go on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock star' reads as a musician, but 'Rock' is the anagram signal on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: To transact business is to carry it out or conduct it.

clue.text: Most tight finishes will get tense

parts.note: closes means ends or finishes
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: The tightest finishes will make everyone nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tense' looks like nervous but is the grammar abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Closest means nearest or most narrow, as in the closest of contests.

clue.text: Old lady sadly returned greeting

indicators.note: returned means read back the other way, bottom to top in a down clue

parts.note: old lady is slang for mother, MA
alas is an expression meaning sadly or unfortunately

explanation.surface: An elderly woman came back and sadly said hello.
explanation.definitionFit: A salaam is a respectful salutation in many Muslim countries, a low bow with the hand to the forehead.

clue.text: Jam sandwiches ordered? The opposite, being cut off

indicators.note: sandwiches means one piece holds another inside it
The opposite flips the order: ordered holds jam, not jam holds ordered

parts.note: bade is the past tense of bid, meaning ordered
to lock is to jam, as with a jammed or locked wheel

explanation.surface: Jam sandwiches were ordered, then the supply was cut off.
explanation.walkthrough: Read plainly, 'Jam sandwiches ordered' puts the ordered word inside the jam word; 'The opposite' tells the solver to swap which one holds the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A blockade is the act of isolating a place by cutting off supplies or access.

clue.text: Composer's comment showing approval of Simpson?

indicators.note: of joins the approval to the Simpson, making the comment about him

parts.note: Bart Simpson, the cartoon boy from The Simpsons
OK is a remark that signals approval

explanation.surface: A composer gives a remark approving of someone named Simpson.
explanation.walkthrough: A famous cartoon schoolboy gets the nod: 'Bart OK'.
explanation.definitionFit: Béla Bartók was a Hungarian composer and pianist of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Spree perhaps in topless club

indicators.note: topless means losing the top letter, in a down clue the first

parts.note: a driver is a golf club for long shots

explanation.surface: A shopping or drinking spree at a topless bar.
explanation.walkthrough: The Spree is a river through Berlin.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spree is a German river, so it is one example of a waterway.

clue.text: Dressed in latex at end of disco for larks

indicators.note: dressed means arranged or prepared, so the letters are set out anew
end of asks for the closing letter of disco

explanation.surface: Someone wore latex at the end of a disco night, just for fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'larks' looks like fun; it is the birds, whose group name is the answer. 'Dressed' scrambles IN LATEX AT plus O from 'end of disco'.
explanation.definitionFit: An exaltation is the traditional collective noun for a flock of larks.

clue.text: Contend with opinion

parts.note: to vie is to contend or compete

explanation.surface: Someone must wrestle with a point of view.
explanation.definitionFit: A view is a belief or attitude, what one thinks about something.

clue.text: Somewhat inebriated gymnast is irritable

indicators.note: Somewhat says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A tipsy gymnast is in a grumpy mood.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgy means tense, nervous and short-tempered, so being edgy is being touchy.

clue.text: Wise folk given case of suspect to judge? Just one of them

indicators.note: given joins the pieces in sequence

parts.note: the Magi were the wise men of the Nativity

indicators.note: case of asks for the outside letters of suspect, its casing

parts.note: to rate is to judge or assess

explanation.surface: Wise people take a suspect's case to a judge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'judge?' looks like the definition, but it gives RATE; 'Just one of them' then says the answer is only one kind of judge.
explanation.definitionFit: A magistrate is a lay judge in lower courts, one sort among many who sit in judgement.
